Choosing a D&D gift for a player or game master

By Couple Better Gifts · Updated October 5, 2026 · How we choose gifts

Find out whether they’re a player, a game master, or both. A player might use a character journal; a game master might need room for session notes, maps, and several characters. Also ask whether they play online or around a table.

Check their role and their table

A player may want a comfortable way to organize one character’s information. A game master may manage encounters, locations, and notes about several people at once. Ask whether their group meets in person or online, and whether they use physical materials or digital tools. A large dice tray may be useful at one table and inconvenient on a small desk shared with a laptop.

Also ask which game and rules version they use before buying a rules-specific journal, book, or reference aid. An item labeled “tabletop” may be generic, while a formatted character journal may assume a particular system. Check sample pages to see whether the layout suits their game.

Dice: readability is part of the gift

The official D&D Basic Rules describe polyhedral dice including d4, d6, d8, d10, d12, and d20. For a set advertised for D&D, read the list of included pieces. Then look at number contrast and how easily the values can be read.

A striking color pattern can make a set fun to receive, but it is less useful if the numbers disappear into the design. Material also changes the feel and weight. If they share a table, consider whether a rolling surface or storage solution better fits their habits than another dice set.

Dice trays and bags

A tray needs enough space for comfortable rolling without occupying the area they use for notes. A collapsible format may make sense for someone who travels to a friend’s home; a permanent setup can suit someone who hosts. Check the unfolded dimensions as well as the packed size.

A dice bag and a dice tray solve different problems. The bag helps with transport and organization. The tray defines a rolling area. If the person already has plenty of dice but carries them loose, storage may be the more useful direction. If they play entirely online, neither may be a priority.

Journals: check the page layout

Read or inspect sample pages. A player-focused journal may emphasize a character’s inventory and abilities. A campaign notebook for a game master needs space for sessions, places, and people. Avoid an elaborate structure that leaves too little room for the kind of notes the recipient writes.

Ask how they remember what happened last session. If they already have a digital system that works, a new paper format may become a burden. Choose a flexible format when you know they like handwritten notes but do not know their exact system.

Miniatures: check the hobby around the game

Miniatures are a more specific purchase than dice. Find out whether their group uses them, what scale fits their existing pieces, and whether the recipient enjoys painting. An unpainted set can be an enjoyable project for a painter and unfinished work for someone who simply wants a piece ready for the table.

Read what the box includes. Do not assume paints, brushes, bases, or other materials are provided. If a figure depicts a particular character or brand, check the maker’s licensing information.

Before ordering

When you know their exact game and preferences, a specialized accessory can feel personal. If you’re unsure, ask what they use at their next session. Confirm current price, dimensions, delivery, and returns before buying.
